stops.name: Hallgrímskirkja
stops.en: This can't miss attraction towers over the city on top of a hill. In front is a statue of Leif Ericsson (Leifur Eiríksson in Icelandic), the Norse explorer who sailed to North America in the 10th century. The United States gave this statue to Iceland in 1930, in honor of the 1,000th anniversary of the Althingi, the Iceland parliament.

stops.name: Icelandic Phallological Museum
stops.en: A museum dedicated to Phallology, the study of penises. This museum features phalluses of numerous animals from various whales to a human specimen.

stops.name: Tjörnin
stops.en: A small lake in the centre of the city where young and old often gather to feed the ducks. The Icelandic name, Tjörnin, literally means "The Pond". Tjörnin is mostly surrounded by a park called Hljómskálagarðurinn (Music Pavilion Park) which gets very popular in good weather. The southern end of Tjörnin links it to the Vatnsmýri swamp, a small bird reserve with paths open to the public except duri

stops.name: Viðey
stops.en: Viðey is a large island in Kollafjörður, the fjord to the north of Reykjavík. It used to be inhabited, and in the early 20th century it had a small fishing village. Nobody lives there anymore apart from the birds, but it's a popular way to get away from the city without leaving it. During the summer, a café is operated in one of the houses on the island. The building was built for Skúli Magnússon,

stops.name: National Museum of Iceland
stops.en: This museum, by the University of Iceland campus, takes the visitor through the history of a nation from settlement to today. Includes a café and a museum shop.

stops.name: Imagine Peace Tower
stops.en: Yoko Ono's memorial to John Lennon, projecting a "tower of light" into the air that can be seen from around Reykjavík. The tower is turned on October 9-December 8, December 21–28, December 31 and March 21–28.

stops.name: Alþingishúsið
stops.en: On the southern edge of Austurvöllur is a small building of hewn stone, but don't let its size fool you. This is the building of the Icelandic parliament, known as Alþingi. The institution has in fact long since outgrown the building which was built in 1881 for a nation of a little over 60,000. Today the upper floors of most houses on the north and west sides of the park also house parliamentary o

stops.name: Landakotskirkja
stops.en: The Catholic cathedral of Iceland.

stops.name: Perlan
stops.en: An iconic building on top of a wooded hill called Öskjuhlíð, to the southeast of the city centre. Perlan is built on top of five hot water storage tanks and offers fantastic views of the entire city from a viewing platform open to the public and from a rotating restaurant at the top. If the restaurant is too expensive for you (it is for most), there is also a small cafeteria on the same floor as t

stops.name: Harpa
stops.en: Harpa is a new concert hall and conference centre at the heart of Reykjavík. It is the home of the Icelandic Symphony Orchestra and regularly host to other acts as well.

stops.name: Reykjavík Cathedral
stops.en: The church beside the parliament is Reykjavík Cathedral, the mother church of the Church of Iceland, the country's national church and part of the Lutheran denomination. Similarly deceptive in size, it has been beautifully renovated both inside and out to reflect its original 18th-century architecture.

stops.name: Reykjavik Art Museum
stops.en: By the old harbour in Reykjavík, Hafnarhúsið hosts a rotating exhibitions of the work of Icelandic artist Erró and temporary exhibitions often showcase other local artists.

stops.name: National Gallery of Iceland
stops.en: The National Gallery of Iceland is a national museum and the main emphasis of the collection is on 20th and 21st century Icelandic art, but international art is featured as well. The museum owns the most valuable collection of works by Icelandic artists in the country.The National Gallery of Iceland regularly holds exhibitions reflecting its collections as well as exhibitions by individual artists

stops.name: Ráðhús Reykjavíkur
stops.en: One of the best examples of late 20th-century architecture in Iceland, built into Tjörnin (The Pond). On the ground floor, which is open to the public, there is a large relief map of the whole country as well as a café and an exhibition hall.

stops.name: Reykjavík Botanic Garden
stops.en: The Reykjavík Botanical Gardens are not large, but they're nice for a short stroll and a good place to see some of the plants that grow in Iceland.

stops.name: Árbæjarsafn
stops.en: In the suburb of Árbær, and frequently called Árbæjarsafn (Árbær museum), this open air museum contains both the old farm of Árbær and many buildings from central Reykjavík that were moved there to make way for construction. The result is a village of old buildings where the staff take you through the story of a city. The staff are dressed in old Icelandic clothing styles and trained in various tr

stops.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Iceland
Grótta
stops.en: At the far western end of the peninsula on which Reykjavík sits there is a small island. This island, called Grótta, is connected to the mainland on low tides and open to the public most of the year (closed May 1-Jul 15). Just make sure you don't get stuck on the island when the tide comes in!

stops.name: Austurvöllur
stops.en: A small park (or square, depending on definitions) in the heart of Reykjavík. It's many locals' favorite place to spend sunny days, either at one of the cafés lining the north of the square or simply having a picnic on the grass. The parliament and the national cathedral both stand by Austurvöllur.

stops.name: Reykjavík Museum of Photography
stops.en: A very small museum with a nice library and reading room where you can find some older (but good) books about photography and current and past issues of photography magazines. It also has a huge collection of Icelandic photographs.

stops.name: Klambratún
stops.en: Klambratún is a park just east of the city centre on an area which remained farmland while the city was built up around it. The area was later converted into one of the largest public parks in the city and often hosts various events. One of the houses of the Reykjavík Art Museum, Kjarvalsstaðir, is inside the park.

stops.name: the Settlement Exhibition
stops.en: Run by the Reykjavík City Museum, this exhibition in central Reykjavík was built around the oldest archaeological ruins in Iceland. As the name indicates, these ruins date to around the year 870. This interactive exhibitions brings you the early history of the area that today forms central Reykjavík.

stops.name: Icelandic Punk Museum
stops.en: A small museum devoted to the history of punk music in Iceland, located in a former underground public toilet facility. In the final room you can listen to Icelandic punk music through headphones, and there are guitars and leather jackets to try on and pose with.

stops.name: Reykjavík Art Museum - Kjarvalsstaðir
stops.en: It is safe to say that Jóhannes Kjarval (1885-1972) is the single biggest name in Icelandic painting. Kjarvalsstaðir hosts a collection of his work, as well as hosting other temporary exhibitions.

stops.name: The House of Collections
stops.en: The House of Collections, built in 1906, has housed all the major Icelandic collections at some point. It houses the semi-permanent exhibition Resistance which is an interdisciplinary exhibition that bridges the gap between visual arts and science. The works include some of the pearls of Icelandic art from the collection of the National Gallery of Iceland. The House of Collections is one of three

eats.name: Bæjarins beztu pylsur
eats.note: The name of this popular hot dog stand literally means "Town's Best Hotdogs" and, based on the queues, it seems to deserve the name.

eats.name: Hamborgarabúllan
eats.note: Small hamburger cafe next to the old harbour designed in the traditional American diner style. Very popular with locals and a reliable alternative to the absent international burger chains.

eats.name: Múlakaffi
eats.note: A bit away from the city centre, this place is very like an office cafeteria. It prides itself on selling authentic Icelandic home cooking. The sparse menu varies between days. Due to its location sur

eats.name: Perlan
eats.note: In addition to its famous restaurant, Perlan also has a café offering food. You can eat with (almost) the same view and a much cheaper price.

eats.name: Sægreifinn
eats.note: An extremely authentic seafood place, serves a wonderful lobster soup and offers grilled cod, whale, shrimps, salmon, etc.

eats.name: Tian
eats.note: This little Chinese restaurant near Laugardalslaug parc and the Arctic Comfort Hotel is a quiet little spot with great food and friendly service. The prices are quite low.

eats.name: Café Haiti
eats.note: A cafe serving coffee and light food. Note that this is not their original location, although you can see their sign still painted on the side of nearby building where they began. They roast their own

eats.name: Kaffismiðja Íslands
eats.note: This cafe supposedly employs some of Iceland's best baristas, and does serve great coffee. Also offers a selection of French and Icelandic pastries. On the small side with just a few tables, but big w

eats.name: Kaffiport
eats.note: The small restaurant inside the flea market is one of the cheapest places to eat in the city. They have kjötsúpa (Icelandic lamb soup), pylsa (hot dogs), some desserts and drinks.

eats.name: Kolaportið
eats.note: If you're in Reykjavik on a weekend, don't miss the farmers market. Many vendors have free samples of Icelandic chocolate, Icelandic liquorice, Icelandic desserts, and even hakarl (fermented shark). E

eats.name: Austur-Indíafjelagið
eats.note: One of few Indian restaurants in Reykjavik. It serves very good food though and can be compared to the top tier Indian restaurants in the UK.

eats.name: Caruso
eats.note: A cozy Italian restaurant with good food. They sometimes have live guitar music, which together with the dimmed lighting makes for a very romantic setting.

eats.name: The Icelandic Bar
eats.note: Serves delicious traditional Icelandic food at reasonable prices, the lamb shank in particular is a must try as is the simple but extremely tasty skyr dessert. Set menus are available from around 4000

eats.name: Restaurant Reykjavik
eats.note: A good central restaurant, aimed a little more toward the tourist crowd it does however deliver decent food. The lamb is good. Also contains an ice bar.

eats.name: Shalimar
eats.note: A small family-owned Pakistani restaurant packed into a tiny building in the oldest part of town. Delicious food, and a very friendly staff.

eats.name: Vegamót
eats.note: A decent fast food restaurant during the day and a happening nightclub after hours. Minimum age of 22 on Friday and Saturday nights. The lobster pasta is the restaurant's signature dish and well worth

eats.name: Þrír frakkar
eats.note: A nice seafood restaurant. Serves big meals for a moderate price. Their lunch plokkfiskur special is legendary. They serve whalemeat, both raw (as sashimi) and cooked, to those willing to try. This is

eats.name: Fjalakötturinn
eats.note: Mostly focuses on fish and seafood, though there are a couple of meat alternatives to choose from. There are also different three and four course menus to choose from and the wine list is more extensi

eats.name: Kaffihús Vesturbæjar
eats.note: Very cosy cafe and bistro. Some tourist but most local clientele. Free Wifi

eats.name: Messinn
eats.note: Generous portions of beautifully cooked fresh fish served in a friendly, warm atmosphere.

eats.name: Dill
eats.note: Part of a growing trend called “new Nordic food” (most famously promoted by Noma restaurant in Copenhagen), this small restaurant prides itself in using local ingredients, many of them sourced from a

eats.name: Fish Company
eats.note: In the basement of a renovated old timber house standing in the original harbour of Reykjavík.

eats.name: Hotel Holt
eats.note: A staple of the city's up-scale dining landscape. Thick carpets, art over dark wood panels, French cuisine, an extensive wine cellar, the country's most expansive collection of single malts.

eats.name: Humarhúsið
eats.note: Specialising in lobster (the name means Lobster House) and on the expensive end, but has exquisite food that the prices reflect.

eats.name: Matarkjallarin
eats.note: Serves excellent modern Western cuisine.

eats.name: Den Danske Kro
eats.note: This place tries to imitate a Danish bodega, although it really feels much more Icelandic than Danish.

eats.name: The English Pub
eats.note: Very popular English-style pub in the heart of the city, with a wide range of beers and a wheel of fortune. Beware troubadours in the weekends, though (they're very bad)!

eats.name: Ölstofa Kormáks og Skjaldar
eats.note: A small, cozy and extremely popular bar. The decorations seem to be taken from the living rooms of Icelandic grandmothers and include a number of cross stitched pictures. Uniquely for Reykjavík bars t

eats.name: Kíkí
eats.note: A friendly gay bar/club on the second and third stories of an old wooden house.

eats.name: b5
eats.note: Caters mainly to a slightly up-market crowd.

eats.name: Dillon Rock Bar
eats.note: Dillon has become quite the attraction for the Icelandic music industry, rockers, students, family folk and famed Hollywood actors over the past decade. During the summertime you can enjoy a cold one

eats.name: Kofinn
eats.note: In a basement on Laugavegur. DJs here play the most popular pop of all eras from the 1960s onwards, songs people can sing along with while they dance.

next.name: Þingvellir National Park
next.note: Þingvellir National Park is located about an hour and a quarter's drive to the east of Reykjavík, here you can see the canyon caused by the Eurasian and North American plates moving apart. It is also home to the original Alþingi (Parliament) and several other

next.name: Hafnarfjörður
next.note: Hafnarfjörður is a town just outside Reykjavík

next.name: Blue Lagoon
next.note: Blue Lagoon (Bláa Lónið in Icelandic language) is a famous and amazing geothermal spa with the water temperature around 40 °C all year round, even in freezing conditions, located south-west of Reykjavík, not far from the main airport at Keflavík.
